title: CCBHC Billing and Documentation in 2026: PPS, Required Services and Audit Risk
summary: What being a CCBHC means for billing and documentation in 2026: the demonstration states, the new state plan option, PPS-1 to PPS-4, what counts as a visit, required quality measures, the records that support PPS claims and where audit risk sits.
body_markdown:
A CCBHC in the Section 223 Medicaid demonstration bills a clinic-specific, cost-based PPS rate, per day under PPS-1 and PPS-3 or per month under PPS-2 and PPS-4, whenever it delivers a qualifying service from the nine required services. To keep that money, the chart must prove each qualifying service and the access timelines in the 2023 certification criteria. As of November 2026, states can also cover CCBHCs under a new state plan option with no PPS mandate.


This guide covers the model's origin and 2026 state list, demonstration vs grant vs state plan CCBHCs, the nine services and DCOs, the PPS methods, quality measures, the documentation behind PPS claims and audit risk, plus a readiness checklist.


The short version


- Demonstration states pay CCBHCs through one of four PPS methods: PPS-1 (daily), PPS-2 (monthly), PPS-3 (daily with separate crisis rates) or PPS-4 (monthly with separate crisis rates).
- Ten states joined the demonstration in 2024. Ten more were announced on May 28, 2026, starting between July 1, 2026 and July 1, 2027. A CMS letter from October 2026 explains the new permanent state plan option, which has no PPS mandate and no enhanced match.
- A PPS visit needs a service on your state's qualifying list, delivered to a Medicaid enrollee by the CCBHC or a DCO. That's one daily rate per person per day, or one monthly rate for a month with at least one service.
- The record has to show the access clock: triage at first contact, an initial evaluation within 10 business days for routine needs, a full evaluation within 60 calendar days and a treatment plan review at least every 6 months.
- Audit risk sits in non-qualifying encounters billed at PPS, cost report errors, DCO oversight, staffing and proof of 24/7 crisis coverage. HHS-OIG has an active audit of demonstration payments.


## Where CCBHCs come from, and which states are in the demonstration in 2026


Section 223 of the Protecting Access to Medicare Act of 2014 (PAMA), enacted April 1, 2014, created the CCBHC demonstration. Starting in 2017, 67 CCBHCs opened in eight states. The CARES Act added two states in 2020. Then the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (BSCA), signed June 25, 2022, let up to ten new states join on July 1, 2024 and every two years after that, and extended the original states through September 30, 2025.


Cohort States Status as of November 2026


**2017 original eight** Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania Pennsylvania withdrew in 2019 and Nevada moved out in 2023. SAMHSA's July 2026 map no longer lists these states in the demonstration. It lists most of them, with Georgia and Texas, as covering CCBHCs through a state plan amendment or section 1115 authority


**2020 (CARES Act)** Kentucky, Michigan In the demonstration


**2024 (BSCA round 1)** Alabama, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Vermont In the demonstration, with start dates between July 1, 2024 and July 1, 2025


**2026 (BSCA round 2)** Alaska, Colorado, Hawaii, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, Washington, West Virginia Announced May 28, 2026, with start dates between July 1, 2026 and July 1, 2027


HHS said the 2026 round brings the states supporting the model through Medicaid or the demonstration to 31, and SAMHSA counts over 500 CCBHCs nationally. A state needs a one-year SAMHSA planning grant before it can compete. In January 2025, 14 states and Washington, D.C. received $1 million planning grants, and the BSCA schedule points to 2028 as the next window.


## Demonstration, expansion grants and state-certified CCBHCs


"CCBHC" now describes clinics paid in very different ways. The label on your door matters less than the authority your state uses, because that decides whether you get a PPS rate at all.


Route Who certifies How Medicaid pays Federal match


**Section 223 demonstration** The state, against SAMHSA's criteria Required PPS, one of four methods Enhanced, generally equal to the state's CHIP rate


**New state plan option** (Social Security Act 1905(a)(31)) The state, against the most recent criteria State's choice: fee schedule, bundled rate or a PPS-style bundle Regular match


**Other Medicaid authorities** (rehabilitative services, clinic services, 1915(i), 1115) The state Existing approved methods, often several authorities combined Regular match


**SAMHSA expansion grants** The clinic self-attests, though some states certify Grant funds, plus Medicaid through existing methods. No PPS unless the clinic is also demonstration-certified Regular match on Medicaid claims


The state plan option came from section 209 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, enacted March 9, 2024. CMS explained it in State Medicaid Director Letter 26-004 on October 6, 2026. Electing states must submit a state plan amendment, cover all nine services and report the same quality measures as the demonstration, but they don't have to send CCBHC cost reports to CMS.


Grants continue alongside. SAMHSA's FY 2026 CCBHC Improvement and Advancement notice (SM-26-015), posted June 17, 2026, anticipated 117 awards of up to $1 million a year for up to four years to sustain existing CCBHCs.


## The nine required services and DCO arrangements


1. Crisis mental health services, including 24-hour mobile crisis teams, emergency crisis intervention and crisis stabilization
2. Screening, assessment and diagnosis, including risk assessment
3. Person-centered and family-centered treatment planning, including risk assessment and crisis planning
4. Outpatient mental health and substance use services
5. Outpatient primary care screening and monitoring of key health indicators and health risk
6. Targeted case management (called intensive case management under the new state plan option)
7. Psychiatric rehabilitation services, including supported employment, education and housing supports
8. Peer supports, counselor services and family supports
9. Intensive, community-based mental health care for members of the armed forces and veterans


PAMA excludes inpatient care, residential treatment, room and board and other non-ambulatory services from CCBHC services. A residential day never triggers a CCBHC PPS payment.


A Designated Collaborating Organization (DCO) is an outside entity with a formal relationship to the CCBHC that delivers one or more required services under the same standards. The CCBHC stays responsible for access to every service and must deliver at least 51% of encounters directly, excluding crisis services.


CMS's PPS guidance treats DCO encounters as CCBHC encounters and puts DCO costs in the rate. Only one payment may be made for a service, and required services must be billed by and paid to the CCBHC.


## SAMHSA certification criteria in 2026


SAMHSA released updated certification criteria in March 2023, and most CCBHCs had to comply by July 1, 2024. As of SAMHSA's page updated January 21, 2026, the 2023 criteria are still current. They're organized into six program areas: staffing, availability and accessibility, care coordination, scope of services, quality and other reporting, and organizational authority and governance.


Four requirements are easy to let slip. The community needs assessment and staffing plan must be updated at least every three years. The management team needs a psychiatrist as Medical Director, or a medically trained behavioral health professional with prescriptive authority if the clinic can't recruit one after reasonable efforts. An independent financial audit runs every year. And the clinic must be licensed, certified or accredited for both mental health and SUD services.


That last point is where accreditation comes in. CMS told states they may rely on recognized accrediting organizations with CCBHC accreditation programs when they certify clinics, and CARF accredits CCBHCs as a Behavioral Health core program. Our[CARF accreditation guide](https://blog.adentris.com/carf-accreditation-behavioral-health/) covers the survey process, timeline and cost.


## How CCBHC PPS works: PPS-1 to PPS-4


The PPS is a clinic-specific rate built from the CCBHC cost report: total allowable annual costs, direct plus allocated indirect, divided by annual visits. In CMS's simplest example, $10,000 in costs over 100 daily visits gives a $100 daily rate. The state's chosen method applies for the whole demonstration year and can't change without CMS approval. CMS's February 2024 guidance applies from January 1, 2024 for existing states and July 1, 2024 for states added in 2024 and 2026.


Method Unit Crisis rates Special population rates Outlier payments Quality bonus payments


**PPS-1** Daily None None None Optional


**PPS-2** Monthly None Optional Required Required


**PPS-3** Daily Required, separate daily rates None None Optional


**PPS-4** Monthly Required, separate monthly rates Optional Required Required


### What counts as a visit


- **Daily methods.** A visit is a day on which a Medicaid enrollee receives at least one CCBHC service. The clinic gets one PPS payment per person per day, whatever the intensity.
- **Monthly methods.** A visit is a month with at least one CCBHC service, with up to 12 monthly visits per person a year. The state may pay only after a service has been delivered.
- **Qualifying services.** CMS asks states to publish a scope of services and activities list showing which services trigger a visit. Indiana, for example, sorts codes into "triggerable," "overlap" and "non-triggerable" lists.
- **Crisis rates.** Under PPS-3 and PPS-4, states set separate rates for ARP section 9813 qualifying mobile crisis, other mobile crisis and on-site crisis stabilization.


### Rate updates, quality bonuses and cost reports


States update rates every year by the Medicare Economic Index or by rebasing. They must rebase for demonstration year 3 using year 2 cost data, then at least every three years. Quality bonus payments are optional under PPS-1 and PPS-3 and required under PPS-2 and PPS-4. A state paying them must include seven comparative measures, and no bonus may be paid for reporting alone.


Each CCBHC sends its cost report to the state within six months after the demonstration year ends, and the state sends it to CMS within nine months. Uncompensated care shortfalls stay out of the rate. Source documents, including patient records and invoices, must follow federal and state retention rules. Overstated costs or undercounted visits inflate the rate, so reconcile the visit count as carefully as the costs.


### What the claim looks like


CMS lists HCPCS T1040 (Medicaid certified community behavioral health clinic services, per diem) and T1041 (per month). It says the Q2 modifier can carry service-level data and expects claims to include all detail lines.


Indiana's November 2024 bulletin shows how one state applies that. Each claim carries exactly one unit of T1040 at the clinic's PPS rate, at least one triggerable code and every other service that day, with Q2 on encounter lines or V2 when a DCO delivered the service. A claim with no triggerable code is denied. The detail lines use ordinary CPT and HCPCS codes, like those in our[CPT codes for behavioral health guide](https://blog.adentris.com/cpt-codes-behavioral-health-guide/) .


## Required quality measures and data reporting


Group Measures Who reports, and when


**Clinic-collected, required (5)** Time to Services (I-SERV), Depression Remission at Six Months (DEP-REM-6), Unhealthy Alcohol Use Screening and Brief Counseling (ASC), Screening for Clinical Depression and Follow-Up Plan (CDF-CH and CDF-AD), Screening for Social Drivers of Health (SDOH) The CCBHC, for everyone it serves, nine months after the measurement year ends


**State-collected, required (13)** Patient and youth/family experience of care surveys, SAA-AD, FUH-AD, FUH-CH, IET-AD, FUM, FUA, PCR-AD, ADD-CH, AMM-BH, OUD-AD, GSD-AD The state, for Medicaid enrollees, mostly from claims and encounter data


**Optional** Tobacco screening (TSC), suicide risk assessment (SRA), WCC-CH, CBP-AD, and two state-collected antipsychotic measures for children As the state requires


The state submits clinic and state measures to SAMHSA in one annual submission, 12 months after the measurement year ends. Demonstration states also send CCBHC claims or encounter data through T-MSIS. At minimum, that means a unique person identifier, clinic identifier, date of service, CCBHC service, units and diagnosis. A missing field weakens both the evaluation and the state's claim for enhanced match.


## Documentation that supports PPS billing


The PPS hides the detail. Every day or month pays the same rate, so the claim alone can't show that a qualifying service happened, who delivered it or whether the access clock was met. The chart has to.


Record element What it must show Why it matters


**Qualifying service note** Date, service, rendering staff and credentials, CCBHC or DCO, location and modality, signature It's the evidence for the daily or monthly visit and for the modifier on the line


**Triage at first contact** Preliminary triage with risk assessment, and the acuity it found Criteria 2.b.1. The first contact date anchors I-SERV


**Initial evaluation** Completed within one business day for urgent needs or 10 business days for routine needs Timely access criteria and I-SERV


**Full evaluation** Completed within 60 calendar days of the first request Criteria 2.b.1, the basis for the plan


**Treatment plan** Built with and endorsed by the person, including crisis planning and releases of information, reviewed at least every 6 months Criteria 2.b.2 and 4.e


**Screenings** Depression with follow-up, unhealthy alcohol use, social drivers of health, depression scores for remission tracking Clinic-collected measures and quality bonus eligibility


**Crisis encounters** Dispatch and arrival times, intervention, follow-up Mobile teams are expected within one hour, two in rural and frontier areas, never over three hours


**Medical necessity** Diagnosis, functional impairment and why this service now Medicaid coverage rules still apply under a PPS


That last row is easy to forget. A PPS rate doesn't waive the payer's coverage rules, and our[medical necessity documentation guide](https://blog.adentris.com/medical-necessity-documentation-behavioral-health/) covers what reviewers expect. For SUD records shared with DCOs, the criteria tell CCBHCs to obtain and document consent, which brings 42 CFR Part 2 into the workflow.


## Where CCBHC audit risk sits


On November 17, 2025, HHS-OIG announced an audit of CCBHC Medicaid reimbursement (project OAS-25-06-109). It will determine whether selected states claimed expenditures eligible for the enhanced match and whether selected CCBHCs provided the services required to receive Medicaid payment. It's listed as active. State program integrity units, managed care plans and cost report reviewers look at the same issues. Our guide to[Medicare and Medicaid audits in behavioral health](https://blog.adentris.com/medicare-medicaid-audits-behavioral-health/) explains who can review you.


Risk What goes wrong Control


**Non-qualifying encounters at PPS** PPS billed on a day with only non-triggerable services, two daily rates for one person, a monthly rate with no qualifying service, residential or inpatient days, or services at a satellite opened after April 1, 2014 Pre-bill check that every PPS claim has a triggerable service backed by a signed note


**Duplicate payment** A DCO bills Medicaid for a service that's also counted toward the CCBHC's PPS DCO agreements that state who bills, and a monthly match of DCO activity to claims


**Cost report errors** Unallowable costs, uncompensated care shortfalls in the rate, misallocated indirect costs, visit counts that don't match paid claims Reconcile cost report visits to claims and keep source documents


**DCO oversight** DCO services below criteria standards, no data for quality measures, missing consents Annual DCO review and data-sharing terms in every agreement


**Staffing** No documented Medical Director arrangement, a staffing plan older than its three-year limit, credential gaps Staffing plan tied to the current needs assessment, credential file audits


**24/7 crisis coverage** No proof of round-the-clock availability or response times Dispatch logs, on-call schedules and call center agreements kept for each month


The OIG objective is worth reading twice. It asks whether clinics "provided the services required," and a rate paid for a day says nothing about that. Only the record does.


Coverage churn adds a second exposure. H.R. 1's Medicaid work requirements are set to begin January 1, 2027, and every enrollee who loses coverage is a visit the PPS no longer pays. Plan for it with our[work requirements guide](https://blog.adentris.com/medicaid-work-requirements-behavioral-health/) .


## CCBHC billing and documentation readiness checklist


Area Check Evidence to keep


Authority Confirm whether the clinic is paid under the demonstration, the state plan option, another authority or a grant State certification letter, provider agreement, grant notice


Qualifying services Billing team has the state's current trigger list and PPS method Dated copy of the state code list and billing manual


Claim build One PPS unit per day or month, detail lines for every service, correct modifiers for DCO work Claim edit rules and a monthly sample review


Access clock Triage, initial evaluation, full evaluation and plan review dates tracked per person Report of open clients past 10 business days, 60 days or 6 months


Quality data Five required clinic-collected measures captured in structured fields Measure specifications and a quarterly data check


Crisis 24/7 coverage and response times documented Dispatch logs, schedules, call center agreement


DCOs Formal agreement, same standards, data access, billing terms Signed agreements and annual review notes


Staffing Needs assessment and staffing plan under three years old, Medical Director in place Current assessment, plan and credential files


Cost report Visits reconcile to claims, costs follow federal cost principles, due six months after the year ends Trial balance, allocation workpapers, source documents


Audit Annual independent financial audit done and findings closed Audit report and corrective action plan

SUD chart audit scorecard (Excel)


24 audit items scored across 10 charts. Run it on your SUD charts before a state recertification review or cost report season.

## Frequently asked questions


**What is a CCBHC?**


A Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic is a clinic certified by its state, or self-attested under a SAMHSA grant, as meeting SAMHSA's CCBHC criteria. It must deliver nine required mental health and substance use services, directly or through DCOs, and serve anyone who asks for care regardless of ability to pay or place of residence.


**How does CCBHC PPS billing work?**


In the Section 223 demonstration, the state pays each CCBHC a cost-based, clinic-specific rate. Under PPS-1 and PPS-3 the clinic bills one rate per person per day with a qualifying service. Under PPS-2 and PPS-4 it bills one rate per person per month with at least one service. PPS-3 and PPS-4 add separate crisis rates.


**What are the nine required CCBHC services?**


Crisis services, screening and assessment, person-centered treatment planning, outpatient mental health and substance use services, primary care screening and monitoring, targeted case management, psychiatric rehabilitation, peer and family supports, and intensive community-based care for members of the armed forces and veterans.


**Which states are in the CCBHC demonstration in 2026?**


SAMHSA lists Alabama, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Rhode Island and Vermont. Alaska, Colorado, Hawaii, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, Washington and West Virginia were announced on May 28, 2026 and start between July 1, 2026 and July 1, 2027.


**What is a DCO in a CCBHC?**


A Designated Collaborating Organization is an outside provider with a formal agreement to deliver one or more required services under the same standards as the CCBHC. DCO encounters count as CCBHC encounters for the PPS, the CCBHC stays responsible for access and bills the service, and at least 51% of non-crisis encounters must be delivered directly.


**Do CCBHCs have to file cost reports?**


Demonstration CCBHCs do. Each clinic submits an annual cost report to the state within six months after the demonstration year ends, and the state forwards it to CMS within nine months. States covering CCBHCs under the new state plan option aren't required to send cost reports to CMS, though they may use one to set rates.
